questions.question: How should a physical query plan generally be read?
options: From leaf scans upward through operators to the result
From the SQL keywords alphabetically to the table names
From the highest estimated cost directly to the lowest
From the final LIMIT backward while ignoring input scans

questions.question: Which join is strong for a small outer input probing an indexed inner key?
options: Full Cartesian join
Nested-loop join
Unordered merge join
Global cross shuffle

questions.question: A date predicate retains 1% of 100 million orders. Where should filtering occur in a good plan?
options: After joining and aggregating all 100 million rows
After final ORDER BY and LIMIT return results
At partition pruning or near the orders scan
Inside the client after the database transfers every row

questions.question: What does a large gap between estimated and actual rows often explain?
options: Why the query returned fewer rows than the application expected
Why the reported cost units differ between two database products
Why a join produced duplicate rows despite a unique declared key
Why the optimizer chose an algorithm unsuited to real cardinality

questions.question: Why can DATE(created_at) = a date be less sargable than a half-open timestamp range?
options: Applying a function can prevent direct navigation of a raw timestamp index
Half-open ranges always read the complete table regardless of index
DATE converts every timestamp into a primary-key uniqueness constraint
Timestamp indexes support equality but never ordered range searches

questions.question: A hash aggregate spills to disk. What should be investigated first?
options: Whether the grouping columns are declared NOT NULL in the source
Whether input cardinality, row width, or memory caused the overflow
Whether the client fetches the result in one batch rather than pages
Whether the output column aliases collide with base column names

questions.topic: B-tree Database Index vs Inverted Search Index
questions.question: What does a B-tree database index primarily organize?
options: Token positions from every text field
Vector neighbors by approximate distance
Ordered row-key values and row references
Complete model outputs by generation temperature

questions.topic: B-tree Database Index vs Inverted Search Index
questions.question: What does an inverted index map?
options: Rows to ordered scalar primary keys only
Documents to one complete unparsed body string
Timestamps to database pages in date order
Terms to postings of matching documents

questions.topic: B-tree Database Index vs Inverted Search Index
questions.question: Why does a B-tree on the full body text not efficiently answer contains the term retrieval?
options: It orders complete strings rather than indexing interior terms
B-trees store text keys only when the column is declared UNIQUE
It tokenizes the body but then discards every postings list
A B-tree can compare strings only for equality, never for ordering

questions.topic: B-tree Database Index vs Inverted Search Index
questions.question: An index is ordered by tenant_id, created_at. Which predicate best matches its leading layout?
options: Body text contains a token with no tenant constraint
Tenant equality plus a created-at range
Created-at range across all tenants with no tenant value
Cosine similarity across document embeddings

questions.topic: B-tree Database Index vs Inverted Search Index
questions.question: A query combines BM25 text matching with tenant and status constraints. What design is appropriate?
options: Use the relevance score itself as the authorization boundary
Store the tenant and status values as prose in the document body
Maintain text postings plus structured access paths, then intersect
Replace the term postings with a single complete-body B-tree key

questions.topic: B-tree Database Index vs Inverted Search Index
questions.question: Why do both B-trees and inverted indexes amplify writes?
options: Both store a second copy of every row alongside the base table
Both require a complete table scan before each point lookup
Both discard ordering on insert and rebuild it lazily at read time
Both maintain extra structures through page splits or segment merges

questions.question: Which ACID property makes a debit and credit commit together or not at all?
options: Atomicity
Consistency
Isolation
Durability

questions.question: Which ACID property protects concurrent operations from invalid interleavings according to an isolation level?
options: Atomicity
Isolation
Durability
Compression

questions.question: A commit succeeds but its acknowledgment is lost and the client times out. What should the client infer?
options: The transaction definitely rolled back
The database definitely deleted all prior writes
The outcome is uncertain, so a retry needs idempotency
Durability guarantees the client received the response

questions.question: Why should remote API calls usually stay outside a retryable database transaction?
options: A transaction cannot issue any network request from inside its body
A remote call inherits the transaction's rollback, so it is undone too
The database releases its row locks automatically while a remote call runs
Retries may repeat irreversible effects and long calls raise contention

questions.question: How should a massive index rebuild use atomicity without one enormous transaction?
options: Build and validate a version separately, then atomically switch a small alias
Expose partially written files and update the public alias after every chunk
Hold one database lock while embedding the complete corpus for several days
Mutate the serving index in place without a version or rollback target

questions.question: Why does ACID not make a workflow across Firestore, GCS, Pub/Sub, and an API globally atomic?
options: ACID applies only to read operations and never to writes
Each system has its own transaction boundary and failure contract
Durability removes the need for reconciliation between systems
Isolation automatically creates a distributed transaction across products

questions.question: Which workload is characteristic of OLTP?
options: Scanning five billion events for a monthly percentile
Aggregating all model versions by quarter
Fetching and updating one job by primary key
Joining years of history for a dashboard

questions.question: Why does columnar storage suit OLAP scans?
options: It keeps each complete row together so one row can be fetched fast
It stores each value separately, so repeats cannot be compressed
It must read every column of the table before filtering the rows
It reads only referenced columns and supports vectorized processing

questions.question: Why should a full-table dashboard scan avoid the primary OLTP database when possible?
options: It can evict hot pages and slow latency-sensitive customer writes
An OLTP engine rejects any query that reads more than one partition
A long scan holds write locks on every row it reads until it finishes
Row storage makes a scan read fewer bytes than a columnar store would

questions.question: How can the same orders domain support both workload types?
options: Use the analytical copy as the only authority for order updates
Keep normalized operational truth and a derived analytical copy
Run every point update against compressed immutable warehouse files
Discard change pipelines and accept permanently stale analytics

questions.question: What is the strongest basis for classifying a workload as OLTP or OLAP?
options: The domain the tables belong to, such as orders or events
The product category the vendor assigns the engine in its documentation
Concurrency, transaction needs, selectivity, scan volume, and latency
The storage format the engine happens to use for those tables

questions.question: Which mapping best fits an AI platform?
options: Evaluation history as operational truth and ACLs as an approximate dashboard
All facts in one mutable vector index with no authoritative source
Serving configuration as cold analytics and latency history as transactional state
Jobs and ACLs as operational state; evaluation and cost as analytical facts
